 What to look for How we chose: Reviews compare current prices, published specs, and the recurring complaint patterns across thousands of buyer reviews for each unit, weighing waveform type, real (not just half-load) runtime data, USB shutdown support, outlet topology, and total cost of ownership including battery replacement, not just the sticker price or VA rating.
We judged on: Real wattage draw of a NAS plus router, modem, and switch, not generic bay-count VA tiers · Runtime at a realistic 30-100W combined load, using manufacturer data points closest to that range · Pure sine wave vs stepped sine wave compatibility with active-PFC NAS and PC power supplies · USB shutdown integration path: native NAS UPS settings (NUT), APC PowerChute, or open-source apcupsd · Outlet topology: how many outlets are battery-backed vs surge-only, and how many devices actually fit · Total cost of ownership including battery replacement interval and audible alarm complaints · Current pricing, buyer rating, and the specific complaint pattern in the review history for each unit.
 If your NAS is holding the only copy of ten years of photos, or your router is the thing that keeps a security camera recording, "put it on a battery backup" is not optional advice, it is a missing step. The problem is that most buying guides stop at that sentence. They hand you a VA number tied to bay count and move on, without telling you what your NAS, router, modem, and switch actually draw together, how many real minutes that buys you, or how to make the NAS shut itself down cleanly instead of just dying when the battery runs out. This guide covers all three: sizing, runtime at a realistic load, and the automatic shutdown setup that makes a UPS more than an expensive surge protector.
 The short version
 Best overall: the CyberPower CP1500PFCLCD covers a NAS plus a full network stack with true pure sine wave and a 1000W ceiling for roughly $200 to $250, at roughly half the price of comparable APC Smart -UPS output.
 Best for hands-off NAS shutdown: the APC Back-UPS Pro BX1500M has a dedicated USB data port and the longest runtime here, but expect to configure open-source shutdown software yourself.
 The catch: none of these units talk to a Synology or QNAP NAS out of the box the way a smart plug does. You will spend 15-30 minutes in a settings menu or a config file no matter which one you buy.
 Price reality: a real whole-shelf setup (NAS, router, modem, switch) runs roughly $65 to $240 depending on runtime and waveform, plus a replacement battery every 3-5 years that you should budget for now, not discover later.
 What to Look For
 Size it by what your gear actually draws, not by bay count. Every generic chart pairs "1-2 bay NAS" with a VA tier and stops, which ignores that most people want one UPS covering the whole shelf: NAS, router, cable modem, switch, and sometimes a PoE access point. Add up the rated wattage printed on each device's power brick or label, not a guess. A 2-bay NAS with two spinning drives typically pulls 20-30W; a 4-bay unit with four drives runs 40-60W under load. A router and modem are usually 10-15W each, and an unmanaged switch is 5-10W (a PoE switch feeding an access point can add 15-30W more). Total that up, then multiply by roughly 1.3-1.5 for headroom, since spin-up current spikes higher than steady-state draw and you'll likely add a device later. For most NAS-plus-network shelves, that lands in the 50-110W real-world range, far below the 300-500W people picture when they see a "1500VA" label. Buy for the wattage figure, not the VA number, since VA overstates what a UPS can actually deliver to a non-unity-power-factor load like a switching power supply.
 Runtime claims mean little unless the load matches yours. Manufacturers publish runtime at a generic 100W or half-load test point, and a real NAS-plus-network shelf usually draws less than that, so real runtime is typically longer than the spec sheet implies. The one exception worth calling out: APC publishes a 100W data point for the BX1500M, 68 minutes, which is close enough to a real combined load to use as an actual buying signal instead of a guess.
 Pure sine wave matters if your NAS or PC uses an active-PFC power supply. Most current NAS units and desktop PSUs do. On battery power, a stepped or "simulated" sine wave UPS can cause an active-PFC supply to hum, throw a fault, or in some cases shut down instead of riding through the outage. Pure sine wave costs more, but it is the safer default if you don't know your NAS's PSU type.
 Automated shutdown is what turns a UPS from insurance into protection. A NAS that loses power mid-write risks a corrupted filesystem or a failed RAID rebuild, so the goal is a graceful shutdown before the battery empties, ideally with the NAS shutting down before the router drops so you don't lose remote visibility mid-sequence. Every unit here connects over USB to trigger this, but the software path differs: Synology and QNAP both have native UPS support in their DSM/QTS settings that talks to a directly connected UPS over USB using the NUT protocol, no extra install required. For APC units, the bundled PowerChute software doesn't officially list NAS operating systems as supported, so plenty of owners run open-source apcupsd or NUT instead, which is a config-file job, not a GUI installer. Budget a real chunk of time for this step regardless of which UPS you buy.
 Outlet topology and battery replacement are the two things people forget to check. Every unit here splits its outlets into battery-backed (for the NAS, router, modem, switch) and surge-only (for anything that doesn't need runtime, like a printer or a lamp), and the battery-backed count is the real ceiling on how much gear you can protect, not the total outlet count. Separately, every lead-acid UPS battery degrades and needs replacing every 3-5 years, a recurring $30-60+ cost that's easy to forget when comparing sticker prices. If the unit will live in a bedroom or home office, also check for audible alarm complaints. Several models here can be muted, but owners report the alarm resetting to on after a firmware update or a power event.

 The Bottom Line
 For most people covering a NAS plus a full network stack, the CyberPower CP1500PFCLCD is the right default: pure sine wave, a 1000W ceiling, and the most outlets here for a price that undercuts comparable APC Smart-UPS units by hundreds of dollars. If your priority is the longest possible runtime and you don't mind setting up apcupsd or NUT yourself, the APC Back-UPS Pro BX1500M gets you 68 minutes at a realistic load for less money, at the cost of a stepped waveform. If you're specifically on Synology's PowerChute-integrated ecosystem and want USB-C, the APC Back-UPS Pro BR1500MS2 is the pick, but register it and confirm current firmware given the documented early-failure reports on this model family. A single-bay NAS with a router doesn't need 1500VA: the CyberPower CP850PFCLCD gives you clean pure sine wave for less. And if all you need is to keep the internet up during a blip while a bigger unit handles the NAS separately, the APC Back-UPS BE600M1 is the cheapest way to do that. Whichever you buy, don't stop at the purchase: go into your NAS's UPS settings (or install apcupsd/NUT) and actually configure the shutdown trigger, since an unplugged battery backup only buys you time, not protection.
Frequently asked questions
 What size UPS (VA/W) do I need for my NAS? Skip the generic bay-count chart and add up what your gear actually draws: a 2-bay NAS with two spinning drives typically pulls 20-30W, a 4-bay NAS runs 40-60W, and a router, modem, and switch usually add another 25-45W combined. Multiply that total by 1.3-1.5 for headroom and buy for the resulting wattage figure, not the VA number, since VA overstates what a UPS can deliver to a switching power supply. Most NAS-plus-network setups land in the 50-110W range, which every unit in this roundup covers comfortably. 
 How long will a UPS keep a NAS running during a power outage? Manufacturers publish runtime at a generic 100W or half-load test point, which is higher than most NAS-plus-network setups actually draw, so real runtime tends to run longer than the spec implies. The most useful real-world data point here is the APC Back-UPS Pro BX1500M's own spec: 68 minutes at 100W and 19 minutes at 300W. Treat a UPS as a bridge to a graceful shutdown, not a way to ride out an hours-long outage. 
 Do I need a pure sine wave UPS for a NAS or PC with an active-PFC power supply? Yes, if you know or suspect your NAS or PC has an active-PFC power supply, which most current models do. On battery power, a stepped or simulated sine wave UPS can cause an active-PFC supply to hum, throw a fault, or shut down unexpectedly instead of riding through the outage. Pure sine wave costs more but removes that risk entirely. 
 How do I set up automatic safe shutdown of my NAS when the UPS battery gets low? Synology and QNAP both have native UPS support built into their DSM/QTS settings that talks to a directly connected UPS over USB using the NUT protocol, no extra software required. For APC units, the bundled PowerChute software doesn't officially support NAS operating systems, so most owners configure open-source apcupsd or NUT instead, which is a config-file step rather than a simple installer. Either way, plan for 15-30 minutes of setup after the UPS arrives, and sequence it so the NAS shuts down before the router drops. 
 APC vs CyberPower: which is better for a NAS and network gear? Neither brand wins outright; it depends on what you're optimizing for. CyberPower's CP1500PFCLCD gives you pure sine wave and the most outlets at a lower price than APC's pure sine options. APC's Back-UPS Pro BX1500M wins on runtime per dollar and has a dedicated USB shutdown port, but ships with stepped sine wave. UPS for a NAS: Sizing, Shutdown and Auto Restart | Power Fallback 
 Skip to content 
 UPS for a NAS: Protect Your Data, Shut Down Cleanly, Come Back Automatically
 Every NAS should sit on a UPS, but the goal is not long runtime: it is a clean, automatic shutdown before the battery runs out, then an automatic restart when power returns. A small line-interactive unit is enough for most 2 to 8 bay boxes, as long as the shutdown signal is actually connected.
 By Power Fallback Editorial Team · Reviewed under our editorial standards · Updated October 4, 2026 
 Key takeaways
 A typical 2 to 4 bay NAS draws roughly 15 to 45 W idle and 30 to 70 W under load, so a 600 to 1000 VA UPS usually gives 20 minutes or more.
 The UPS only protects your data if the NAS gets a shutdown signal, over USB from the UPS or over the network from a NUT server.
 Shut down after a fixed time on battery (often 2 to 5 minutes), not at low battery: aged batteries hit low battery far sooner than the estimate says.
 Enable the NAS option to power on when AC returns, and make sure the UPS actually cuts and restores its output, or the NAS can stay off after a short outage.
 Put the switch and router the NAS clients use on the same UPS, otherwise network clients cannot hear the shutdown order.
 On this page What actually goes wrong when a NAS loses power 
 How much power a NAS draws 
 Worked example: a 4-bay NAS with its network 
 Getting the shutdown signal to the NAS 
 Shutdown timing: build a budget 
 Safe mode, power-off and auto restart 
 Choosing the UPS 
 Common mistakes 
 When a UPS is not the whole answer 
 Frequently asked questions 
 What actually goes wrong when a NAS loses power
 A NAS rarely loses its whole volume from one power cut. The damage is usually quieter: a file that was being written is truncated, a database inside a container is left inconsistent, or a parity array has to run a long consistency check after reboot. The risk compounds with every unplanned cut, and some of it is invisible until you need the data.
 Write caches at three levels
 Data headed for disk sits in volatile memory at several points: the operating system's page cache (often several seconds of writes), any SSD read-write cache you have configured, and each hard drive's own onboard DRAM cache. A filesystem that issues flush commands correctly will survive losing the in-flight data, but the application that thought it had saved a file may not. Consumer SSDs used as NAS write caches typically lack power-loss protection capacitors, which is one reason several NAS makers warn about read-write SSD caching without a UPS.
 The RAID write hole
 In RAID 5 and RAID 6 (including hybrid schemes built on them, such as Synology SHR), updating a stripe means writing data blocks and a parity block. Those writes are not atomic. If power fails between them, parity no longer matches data, and the array cannot tell which is wrong. Nothing looks broken until a drive fails and the rebuild reconstructs garbage from the stale parity. Some implementations mitigate this (a journal or partial parity log), and copy-on-write designs like ZFS RAIDZ avoid it by never overwriting live blocks, but a clean shutdown sidesteps the problem entirely.
 Filesystem and metadata integrity
 Journaled filesystems (ext4, XFS) and copy-on-write filesystems (Btrfs, ZFS) are designed to remount consistently after a crash. "Consistent" means the metadata is intact, not that every recent write survived. After an unclean shutdown many NAS operating systems also schedule a full parity scrub or array resync, which can run for many hours on large drives, during which performance drops and a second failure is more dangerous.
 Our analysis: the real cost of an unclean NAS shutdown is the resync window
 On a four-drive array of 12 TB disks, a post-crash parity check reads every sector of every drive, which typically takes most of a day. That is a day of heavy load on drives the same age as the one most likely to fail next. A UPS that buys three minutes of clean shutdown is mostly buying you out of that window, not out of an instant data loss event.
 How much power a NAS draws
 NAS power draw is dominated by the hard drives. A 3.5-inch drive typically idles at 3 to 6 W and reads or writes at 5 to 9 W; the NAS board, fans and CPU add 10 to 30 W for compact units and more for x86 boxes with a discrete network card. Measure your own unit if you can (see how to measure power draw ), or start from the device power draw database .
 Typical NAS power draw ranges (check your own unit) 
 NAS class Idle (W) Active (W) Spin-up peak (W) 
 2-bay ARM or low-power x86 10 to 20 18 to 30 40 to 60 
 4-bay compact NAS 20 to 35 35 to 60 80 to 120 
 6 to 8 bay desktop NAS 35 to 60 60 to 100 130 to 220 
 DIY TrueNAS or Unraid tower, 8+ drives 60 to 120 100 to 200 200 to 350 
 Spin-up surge
 A 3.5-inch drive pulls roughly 1.5 to 2.5 A from its 12 V rail for a few seconds while the platters accelerate, so 20 to 30 W per drive. Most NAS units stagger spin-up so the peak never stacks fully. This matters for the UPS only at boot, when you are usually back on mains, and when drives wake from spin-down during an outage. It is well inside the surge tolerance of any UPS sized for the steady load, so you do not need to oversize for it.
 Waveform
 Small NAS units with external power bricks are tolerant of simulated sine output. Larger rackmount NAS and DIY servers with active-PFC power supplies can occasionally shut off or buzz on a stepped waveform at the moment of transfer. If your NAS has an internal ATX or server supply, a pure sine UPS removes that risk; see pure vs simulated sine wave .
 Worked example: a 4-bay NAS with its network
 A home has a 4-bay NAS (measured 38 W during normal use), a router (12 W) and a small switch (8 W). The router and switch must be on the UPS so other devices can keep reaching the NAS and so network shutdown signals get through. Total: 58 W .
 Candidate: a typical 850 VA / 510 W line-interactive unit with one 12 V 9 Ah battery (about 108 Wh nominal).
 Approximate runtime (min) = Battery Wh x Inverter efficiency x 60 / Load W
 New battery: 108 Wh x 0.80 x 60 / 58 W = about 89 minutes . (We use 0.80 rather than 0.90 because small inverters are less efficient at light load.)
 Battery at three years, assuming about 70% of original capacity: 108 x 0.70 x 0.80 x 60 / 58 = about 63 minutes .
 Load as a share of the watt rating: 58 / 510 = 11%. Plenty of headroom for drive wake-ups.
 The NAS needs perhaps 3 minutes to shut down. So the sensible plan is to ride through short blips, then shut down after 5 minutes on battery , leaving well over half the battery in reserve. That reserve is what makes the setup robust when the battery ages and the runtime estimate becomes optimistic. The UPS runtime calculator models battery aging and nonlinear discharge more carefully than this formula.
 Getting the shutdown signal to the NAS
 A UPS without a signal path just delays the crash. There are two ways to deliver the signal.
 NAS shutdown signaling options 
 Method How it works Good for Watch out for 
 USB (HID) UPS USB port to the NAS; the NAS reads battery status directly One NAS, one UPS Only one host can own the USB link; some UPS models are not on the NAS compatibility list 
 Network UPS server (NUT) The USB-connected host shares UPS status on TCP port 3493; other machines subscribe as clients Several NAS units, PCs, hypervisors on one UPS Switch must be on the UPS; server must allow client IPs; credentials must match 
 Network management card (SNMP) Card in the UPS reports over the network Rack and business UPS units Card is an extra cost; NAS must support SNMP UPS mode 
 Most NAS platforms (Synology DSM, QNAP QTS, TrueNAS, Unraid) use Network UPS Tools under the hood, which is why a Synology can act as a UPS server for a TrueNAS box and vice versa. Platform walk-throughs: Synology , TrueNAS , Unraid . QNAP's settings live under its external device or UPS section and follow the same logic.
 If the NAS does not detect the UPS over USB, check the cable (many UPS units use a special USB-A to RJ45 or USB-B cable) and see UPS not detected .
 Shutdown timing: build a budget
 Choose the trigger deliberately. NAS settings typically offer either "after X minutes on battery" or "when the battery reaches low battery". The time-based trigger is more predictable, because a UPS's low-battery estimate is based on a model of a healthy battery and is often too optimistic on an old one.
 Measure the shutdown duration. Trigger a normal shutdown during typical activity and time it until the power draw falls to standby.
 Add client shutdown time. If PCs or a hypervisor use the NAS as storage, they must finish first (see below).
 Set the trigger. A common choice is 2 to 5 minutes on battery. Most outages that end on their own end within a minute or two, so waiting longer mostly spends battery.
 Check the remaining margin. Trigger time plus shutdown time should use no more than about half of your aged-battery runtime estimate.
 Test it. Pull the UPS plug from the wall during a quiet period and watch the whole sequence. Repeat after any software update.
 Multiple clients that depend on the NAS
 If a hypervisor runs VMs from NFS or iSCSI storage on the NAS, the VMs and host must shut down before the NAS, or the VMs lose their disks mid-shutdown. In NUT terms, the NAS that owns the USB link is the primary and the others are secondaries. When the primary decides to shut down it raises a forced-shutdown flag, and by default it waits for secondaries to disconnect (up to a configurable time) before shutting itself down. Give clients a shorter trigger than the NAS, or rely on that wait, but test that the order is right. The homelab server guide covers multi-host ordering in detail.
 Safe mode, power-off and auto restart
 Platforms differ in what "shutdown" means. Synology DSM, for example, can enter a Safe Mode on UPS signal: services stop and volumes unmount, but the unit may not fully power off. Other platforms perform a full OS shutdown. Behavior also differs between software versions, so read the help page for your exact version.
 Then enable restart. On a NAS this is usually a setting such as "restart automatically when power supply issue is fixed" or "restore to previous power state". On a DIY TrueNAS or Unraid build it is the BIOS/UEFI option often called Restore on AC Power Loss set to Power On or Last State .
 The short-outage trap
 Auto power-on only triggers when the NAS sees AC power disappear and come back. Suppose the outage lasts 6 minutes: the NAS shuts down at minute 5, and grid power returns at minute 6 while the UPS is still on battery. The UPS output never dropped, so the NAS stays off until someone presses the button. The fix is to have the UPS turn off its outlets after the shutdown (NUT calls this the kill-power or shutdown-return behavior; vendor tools call it UPS shutdown delay). The UPS then waits for mains, restores output, and the NAS sees a clean power cycle. Test this exact scenario once.
 Choosing the UPS
 Quick sizing guide for NAS setups (aim for 10 to 20 minutes, not hours) 
 Setup Typical total load Reasonable UPS class 
 2-bay NAS plus router 25 to 45 W 600 to 850 VA line-interactive 
 4-bay NAS, router, switch 45 to 90 W 850 to 1000 VA line-interactive 
 8-bay NAS or DIY server, network, small PC 120 to 250 W 1500 VA pure sine line-interactive 
 Rack NAS with redundant PSUs 150 to 400 W 1500 to 2200 VA rack unit, see network rack 
 Prefer a model whose USB HID interface is listed as compatible with your NAS (or in the NUT hardware list). Line-interactive is the right topology for nearly all home NAS use; online units help mainly where mains voltage is chronically unstable.
 Common mistakes
 No data cable. The NAS sits on battery until the UPS dies, then crashes anyway.
 Network gear left off the UPS. NUT clients lose contact with the server the moment power fails and cannot be told to shut down. Some clients treat a lost link as "assume on battery", others do nothing.
 Shutting down at "low battery" on a five-year-old battery. The battery collapses before the shutdown completes. See when to replace a UPS battery .
 Plugging the NAS into a surge-only outlet. Many UPS units have both kinds; only the battery-backed ones carry the load in an outage.
 Never testing. A shutdown chain that has never run is a guess.
 When a UPS is not the whole answer
 A UPS protects against power events, not against the far more common causes of data loss: drive failure, ransomware, accidental deletion and fire. It is not a backup. If the NAS holds the only copy of anything, a second copy elsewhere is worth more than any UPS. And if your goal is keeping a media server streaming through a four-hour outage, a UPS is the wrong tool for the duration: a portable power station or a generator with a UPS in front of it is the better fit.
 Frequently asked questions
 Does a Synology or QNAP NAS need a pure sine wave UPS?
 Usually not. Most small NAS units run from an external power brick or a modest internal supply that tolerates simulated sine output for the few minutes it takes to shut down. Larger rackmount NAS units with active-PFC supplies are safer on pure sine, and pure sine costs little extra at these sizes, so it is a reasonable default if the price gap is small.
 How long does a NAS take to shut down on UPS power?
 Commonly 1 to 5 minutes, depending on how many services, containers and VMs are running and how busy the disks are. Time it yourself: start a manual shutdown during normal activity and watch the wattmeter until it drops to standby. Add that time, plus a margin, to your shutdown delay.
 Can one UPS shut down two NAS units?
 Yes. Connect the UPS by USB to one NAS and enable its network UPS server (NUT based on most platforms). The second NAS runs as a network client pointed at the first one's IP address. The switch between them must also be on the UPS, and the server NAS should allow the client's IP.
 Will my NAS turn back on by itself after a power outage?
 Only if you enable the power-recovery or restore-on-AC option, and only if the NAS sees power disappear and return. If mains comes back while the NAS is shutting down and the UPS never drops its output, the NAS can sit powered off. Configure the UPS to turn its outlets off after the shutdown signal to avoid this.
 Is a ZFS NAS like TrueNAS safe without a UPS?
 Safer than classic RAID, because ZFS writes copy-on-write and does not suffer the RAID 5 write hole. But it still loses the last few seconds of asynchronous writes, any client application can be left with a half-written file, and repeated hard power cuts stress drives and power supplies. A UPS is still recommended.

 How many listings actually tell you the waveform
 Of the 62 in-stock units we track, 36 state an output waveform - 58 %. Of those, 36 say pure sine and 0 say simulated. The remaining 26 say nothing at all.
 The asymmetry is the finding. Pure sine is a selling point and gets printed; a stepped approximation is not and does not. So a silent listing is more likely to be the cheaper waveform than the better one, and we still do not claim to know which - we count it as unknown and tell you to check the datasheet.
 What the NAS actually does when the power goes
 Every NAS operating system worth running has the same three-stage response and it is worth knowing before you shop, because it tells you which specification to care about. Stage one: the UPS reports that mains has failed. Stage two: a countdown, either a fixed period you set or a wait until the UPS reports low battery. Stage three: the NAS stops services, unmounts its volumes and powers down cleanly.
 The whole sequence is a couple of minutes. It is not a strategy for staying online through an outage, and treating it as one is how people end up buying four times the battery they need. A NAS that shuts down cleanly at minute three has fully succeeded. A NAS with a two-hour battery and no data cable has fully failed, just later.
 Synology's implementation lives in Control Panel under Hardware and Power, and their own documentation describes the choice as either a custom delay or waiting until low battery, after which the unit enters Safe Mode. QNAP's QTS exposes the same shape under External Device, with two configurable responses to a power failure: power off after a set period, or enter auto-protection mode, which their documentation describes as stopping all services and unmounting all volumes to protect your data. TrueNAS runs its UPS service on Network UPS Tools and exposes master and slave modes so one machine can watch the UPS and the rest can watch that machine.
 The practical consequence: if you already run TrueNAS, or a Linux box, or anything else that can run NUT, then the vendor compatibility list is much less binding than it looks, because NUT talks to a very large number of units directly.
 NUT, and why we link it instead of reproducing it
 Network UPS Tools is the open-source project that most of this ecosystem quietly rests on. In the project's own words its goal is "to provide support for Power Devices, such as Uninterruptible Power Supplies, Power Distribution Units, Automatic Transfer Switches, Power Supply Units and Solar Controllers", offering a common protocol and set of tools across manufacturers' incompatible ones. It is GPL licensed.
 Its hardware compatibility list is the reference document for this question. At the date we read it, it recorded at least 199 manufacturers and 1,436 device models as known compatible - a very different number from any single NAS vendor's tested list.
 We link that list rather than reproducing it, and the reason is a rule we apply generally: a stale copy of somebody else's compatibility list is worse than a link to the live one. It is maintained upstream, it changes, and a reader who checks our snapshot from months ago and finds their model missing has been actively misled by us. Go to the source: it is the single most useful page on this subject and it is not ours.
 The practical route for most people is simpler than the list suggests. Plug the unit into the NAS by USB, open the UPS settings, and see whether the machine reports a battery. Most modern units present themselves through a generic HID power-device interface and are recognised without any configuration at all. If it appears, you are done. If it does not, the compatibility list is where to look next.
 Sizing for a NAS, and the honest gap in it
 The sizing method is the one on the hub page and it comes from Synology rather than from us: total the real wattage of everything on the UPS, then divide by the unit's output power factor to get the output rating you need. Synology's worked example puts a 650 W total against a 70% power factor and arrives at 928.5 W.
 What we cannot give you is the first number. This site publishes no per-device wattage - not for a four-bay NAS, not for an eight-bay, not for a switch - because we have not fetched and logged a maker datasheet for each machine, and a wattage attributed to a typical device of that shape is not a citation. Your NAS publishes its own figure. On Synology's spec pages it sits under power consumption, usually with two values, one for access and one for hibernation, and a note about the drive configuration it was measured with. That last part matters: the figure moves with how many drives you have fitted, because most of the draw is spinning platters, not the chassis.
 Two additions people forget. Drives spinning up simultaneously at power-on draw substantially more than they do at idle, so a unit sized exactly to the running figure has no headroom for a restart. And the network switch between the NAS and everything else needs to be on the same UPS, or the NAS survives the outage in perfect isolation and nobody can reach it.
 What our own catalogue can tell you is what is on the shelf at each VA band and what real power those units claim - that table is on the hub, it is a measurement of our inventory, and it is labelled as one rather than dressed up as a recommendation about your hardware.
 One UPS, several machines
 The common homelab shape is one UPS carrying a NAS, a switch, and one or two other machines, and the question is how the machines that do not hold the USB cable find out about the outage.
 All three ecosystems solve it the same way, with different names. Synology's compatibility page states it plainly: any model on their list can extend UPS service to a second Synology product using Network UPS Server, where the first machine connects by USB and relays the information to clients on the local network. QNAP exposes network UPS master and slave modes. TrueNAS calls it master and slave and, being NUT underneath, will happily act as either against a non-TrueNAS peer.
 Because they are all speaking the same underlying protocol, mixed environments generally work: a TrueNAS box holding the cable can signal a Linux machine running NUT, and a Synology acting as server can be watched by another Synology. What is not guaranteed is any particular cross-vendor pairing, and we are not going to assert one we have not tested.
 Synology adds one hardware caveat worth repeating because it catches people: connect the USB device directly to a USB port on the product. Connecting through a hub is not supported. If your NAS is behind a hub for want of ports, that is the first thing to eliminate when it fails to see the UPS.
 Test it, because nobody else will
 This is the step that gets skipped and it is the only one that proves the purchase worked. The instruction is not ours - it is on Synology's own compatibility page, attached to the tested list: the UPS power-off function varies by brand and model, so simulate a power outage to ensure the function performs as expected.
 Do it deliberately, on a day when nothing is at stake, with nothing important being written. Pull the mains plug on the UPS - not the switch, the plug - and watch. The NAS should log the loss within seconds, count down, and shut down. Then restore power and confirm it comes back up and remounts cleanly.
 Repeat it after any change to the chain: a new UPS battery, a firmware update on either device, moving the cable to a different port. And repeat it when the battery is around three years old, because a battery that has aged out will still let the NAS see the UPS and report a healthy state right up until the moment it is asked to actually supply power.
 A shutdown chain that has never been tested is a shutdown chain you are guessing about, and the outage is a bad time to find out that the guess was wrong.
 Where to go next
 The UPS hub has the waveform rule and the sizing method in full · Rackmount units if the NAS lives in a rack · NAS devices , the DS925+ and drive compatibility by machine cover the other end of the cable · NAS drives and filling a NAS are the array itself · enclosures share the outlet and want counting into the load.
 Frequently asked questions
 Does my UPS have to be on Synology's compatibility list? No, and the list is narrower than most readers assume. It is category-level rather than per-machine, and a large share of the tested units are regional SKUs built for other mains supplies - Synology lists BR1500MS-TW where the US shelf carries BR1500MS2. Not listed means Synology has not tested that exact SKU; it is not a compatibility verdict. Most modern units present a generic HID power-device interface over USB and are recognised without configuration.
 How much runtime does a NAS need? Minutes, not hours. The job is to notice the outage, stop services, unmount volumes and power down cleanly, which takes a couple of minutes on a normal array. Buying a much larger battery to keep serving files through an outage is a different and much more expensive goal, and it only works if the network switch and everything else in the path are on the same protection.
 Can one UPS shut down more than one machine? Yes. One machine holds the USB cable and relays the state to the others over the network. Synology calls it Network UPS Server, QNAP calls it network UPS master and slave, and TrueNAS calls it master and slave. All three are speaking Network UPS Tools underneath, which is why mixed setups usually work - though we do not assert any specific cross-vendor pairing we have not tested.
 Can I plug the UPS into my NAS through a USB hub? Synology's own guidance says no - connect USB devices directly to a USB port on the Synology product, because connecting via a hub is not supported. If a NAS cannot see a UPS that is otherwise working, a hub in the path is the first thing to eliminate.
 What is NUT and do I need it? Network UPS Tools is the open-source project that provides a common protocol for monitoring power devices across manufacturers, licensed under the GPL. You do not install it on a Synology or QNAP - it is already underneath the vendor's UPS feature. You do use it directly on TrueNAS, Linux and BSD machines. Its hardware compatibility list recorded at least 199 manufacturers and 1,436 models at the date we read it, which is a far broader set than any single NAS vendor's tested list.
 How do I know the shutdown actually works? Test it, and take the instruction from the vendor rather than from us: Synology's compatibility page says the power-off function varies by brand and model and to simulate a power outage to ensure it performs as expected. Pull the mains plug deliberately, on a quiet day, and watch the NAS notice, count down and stop. Repeat after any firmware or hardware change, and again when the battery is a few years old.
 Sources
 Specification claims on this page were checked against the pages below on 4 August 2026 . Where a widely-repeated figure did not survive that check, we report what the source says now and say so in the text rather than repeating the familiar number.
 CyberPower Systems - Active PFC Compatibility (glossary) ( cyberpowersystems.com , 2026-08-20 ) Used for: the maker's own definition, quoted verbatim on our pages: Active PFC compatibility is "a feature of UPS systems that delivers sine wave output to prevent unexpected shutdowns or component stress for connected devices with Active PFC power supplies." This is the source for the spec-gate framing - the failure mode named by the maker is an unexpected shutdown, which is precisely the event a UPS was bought to prevent.

Also the VA-versus-watts caveat in the vendor's own words: "Different manufacturers have different volt-ampere (VA) ratings based on the performance of their UPS. To determine the total power (W) that the UPS can support, we recommend consulting the manufacturer's product manual." Article last updated 1 April 2024.

Also the vendor's own two operational notes, which we quote rather than restate: that any listed model can extend UPS service to a second Synology product over the network, and that "The UPS power-off function varies by brand and model. Please simulate a power outage to ensure the function performs as expected." The list is CATEGORY-level: it does not filter per machine.

 A homelab UPS has one job your desk UPS does not: hold the load steady long enough for a NAS, a Proxmox node, or a ZFS pool to flush its writes and shut down cleanly. Get that wrong and a two-second flicker can mean a corrupted pool or a half-written database. So the choice comes down to two things most “best UPS” lists skip: a pure sine wave output that your server’s power supply will actually accept, and clean integration with Network UPS Tools so the box shuts itself down on low battery.

 There are seven UPS units worth buying for a homelab or NAS in 2026, split by load size and whether you mount it in a rack. Below is where each one wins, the specs we verified against the manufacturer, how to size one from a real watt reading, and a tested NUT setup that turns any of them into a self-protecting box on Proxmox, TrueNAS, Unraid, or a Synology.
 Current as of October 2026. The graceful-shutdown setup below was tested with Network UPS Tools 2.8.1 on Debian 13. 
 The short version
 If you only read one line: get the CyberPower CP1500PFCLCD for a tower homelab, or the CyberPower CP1500PFCRM2U if it lives in a rack. Both are pure sine wave, both are rated 1000W, and both speak NUT over USB. Here is the full set of picks:
 Best overall (tower): CyberPower CP1500PFCLCD. Pure sine, 1000W, the homelab default.
 Best APC pick: APC Back-UPS Pro BR1500MS2. Pure sine from APC without Smart-UPS pricing.
 Best for a serious rack or cluster: APC Smart-UPS SMT1500C. Long runtime, a real management card slot, serviceable batteries.
 Best rackmount: CyberPower CP1500PFCRM2U. 2U, 1000W pure sine, fits a 14-inch-deep rack.
 Best rack runtime: CyberPower OR1500PFCRT2U. 2U, 1050W, 17 minutes at half load, converts to tower.
 Best budget for a single NAS: CyberPower CP1000PFCLCD. Pure sine at the lowest sensible price.
 Best for a low-draw NAS or network shelf: CyberPower CP850PFCLCD. Small, pure sine, cheap.
 How we tested and what actually matters
 Every spec, waveform, and outlet count below was confirmed against the manufacturer’s own product page, and each Amazon listing was checked to confirm it resolves to the exact model and is currently in stock. Prices move constantly, so treat the figures here as ballparks and check the live price before you buy.
 The part we ran ourselves is the software. A UPS is only useful if your server reacts to it, so we built the full Network UPS Tools chain on Debian 13 (the same base Proxmox runs on) and drove it through a real power-loss sequence using NUT’s simulation driver. That let us confirm the exact behaviour you care about: the moment the battery hits the low threshold, upsmon runs the shutdown command. The runtime numbers per model are from the manufacturers’ own runtime calculators and published reviews, not our bench, and we say so where it matters.
 The single spec that separates a server UPS from a gaming-PC UPS is the output waveform . Cheap units output a stepped, blocky approximation of mains power. A modern power supply with Active PFC (every 80 Plus unit, which means basically every server and NAS) can read that stepped output as unstable and either drop the load or shut down the instant the UPS switches to battery, which is the exact moment you needed it to hold. Pure sine wave avoids that entirely. All seven picks are line-interactive units with pure sine output on battery, which is the right topology for a homelab: the CyberPower flagship, for example, lists a typical 4 ms transfer time, fast enough that a PFC supply never notices the switch.

 1. CyberPower CP1500PFCLCD: best overall
 This is the unit in most homelabs, and for good reason. It is pure sine wave, rated 1500VA/1000W, has a tilting LCD that shows live load and runtime, and CyberPower’s USB interface maps straight to NUT’s usbhid-ups driver with zero fuss. With more than eleven thousand ratings it is also the most road-tested pick here.
 CyberPower CP1500PFCLCD: 1500VA/1000W pure sine, six battery-backed outlets, USB-HID. Image: CyberPower. 
 Of its twelve outlets, six are battery plus surge and six are surge only, so a NAS, a switch, and a Proxmox node all get real runtime while the printer and monitor sit on surge protection. A typical homelab drawing 150W will run well past twenty minutes, which is far more than the minute or two you actually need to trigger a clean shutdown.
 Who it’s for: anyone running a tower NAS or one or two homelab mini PCs under about 500W. It is the safe default. Skip it if: you need rack mounting, or you want a UPS with a hot-swappable battery and a network management card.
 2. APC Back-UPS Pro BR1500MS2: best APC pick
 If you would rather be in the APC ecosystem, the Back-UPS Pro BR1500MS2 is the one to get. It is genuine pure sine wave, Active PFC compatible, rated 1500VA/900W, and adds USB-A and USB-C charging ports on the front for phones and small devices. It works with NUT’s usbhid-ups driver, which is the route we recommend over APC’s older apcupsd (more on that below).
 APC Back-UPS Pro BR1500MS2: pure sine, 900W, ten outlets with USB-C charging. Image: APC by Schneider Electric. 
 At 900W its real-power headroom is a touch lower than the CyberPower, which is irrelevant for a 150W to 300W homelab load and only matters if you are powering something hungry. Ten outlets split six battery-backed and four surge-only.
 Who it’s for: buyers who trust the APC name and want pure sine without paying Smart-UPS money. At about $300 it now costs more than the CyberPower flagship for less real output, so pick it for the brand, not the value. Skip it if: you need more than 900W of real output, or you want a serial port or a management-card slot.
 3. APC Smart-UPS SMT1500C: best for a serious rack or cluster
 The Smart-UPS is a different class of machine. It is line-interactive and pure sine like the others, but it is built to be serviced: hot-swap batteries, a SmartSlot for a network management card, SmartConnect cloud monitoring, and the longest runtime of any 1500VA unit here (well over an hour at a light homelab load). If a UPS is protecting a small cluster you cannot afford to lose, this is the one. It has also become hard to buy. Schneider lists it as non-stock in distribution, and new units on Amazon now run around $715 with only a few left at a time, so check stock before you plan around it. If you want the network card anyway, the SMT1500CNC is the same UPS with a network management card preinstalled, in stock at about $1,060.
 APC Smart-UPS SMT1500C: 1440VA/1000W pure sine, hot-swap battery, SmartSlot card option. Image: APC by Schneider Electric. 
 One honest caveat on the name: this is a line-interactive UPS, not an online double-conversion unit. That is the right topology for a homelab, but do not buy it expecting true online conversion. Over USB it drives NUT’s usbhid-ups driver; with a network management card you can monitor it over the network with snmp-ups instead.
 Who it’s for: a serious rack or a multi-node cluster where long runtime and a serviceable, network-managed UPS earn their cost. Skip it if: you are price-driven, because it costs about three times the CyberPower for protection a 150W lab does not strictly need.
 4. CyberPower CP1500PFCRM2U: best rackmount
 For most homelab racks this is now the one to buy. It is the same PFC Sinewave family as the flagship, rated 1500VA/1000W in a 2U chassis, and at about $360 on Amazon it costs a little over half what the OR1500PFCRT2U below is selling for. All eight outlets are battery-backed, the battery is hot-swappable, and typical transfer time is 8 ms, double the tower flagship’s 4 ms but still within what a PFC supply rides through. It speaks the same USB-HID protocol as the rest of the CyberPower line, so the usbhid-ups setup further down applies unchanged.
 CyberPower CP1500PFCRM2U: 1000W pure sine, eight battery outlets, 10.5 inches deep. Image: CyberPower. 
 The detail that matters in a homelab rack is depth. The chassis is only 10.5 inches deep and CyberPower rates it for racks as shallow as 14 inches, which covers the short network racks and wall-mount cabinets most home setups use. It also has a slot for an optional network management card if you later want SNMP. Where it falls short is runtime: CyberPower quotes 10.2 minutes at half load and 3.1 minutes at full load, plenty for a clean shutdown but not for riding out a long outage.
 Who it’s for: a 19-inch rack of mini PCs, a NAS, and a switch that needs pure sine and a clean shutdown at a fair price. Skip it if: you want the UPS to keep the lab running through a 15-minute outage, which is what the next pick is for.
 5. CyberPower OR1500PFCRT2U: best rack runtime
 The OR1500PFCRT2U is the heavier-duty rack option. It is a 2U pure sine wave unit rated 1500VA/1050W (the most real watts of the CyberPower picks here), it converts between rack and tower with the included hardware, and it uses the same usbhid-ups path we tested. Eight outlets, all battery-backed. The reason to pay more for it is the battery: CyberPower quotes 17 minutes at half load and 7.7 minutes at full load, against 10.2 and 3.1 for the CP1500PFCRM2U. That extra runtime comes at a cost of 15.3 inches of depth and 50.6 lb, so measure the rack first.
 CyberPower OR1500PFCRT2U: 1050W pure sine in a 2U rack/tower chassis. Image: CyberPower. 
 If you want maximum watts in 2U, the Tripp Lite SMART1500RM2U pushes 1350W of pure sine in the same height and accepts an optional SNMP card, but it is an older design and now sells for around $910. For most racks one of the two CyberPowers is the better buy.
 Who it’s for: a rack where you want the lab to ride through short outages, not just shut down. It is running low on Amazon stock, so check availability. Skip it if: the rack is shallow, or the UPS sits next to your desk, because rack units have audible charger and fan noise.
 6. CyberPower CP1000PFCLCD: best budget for a single NAS
 A four-bay NAS plus a 2.5GbE switch rarely draws more than 150W, and for that the CP1000PFCLCD is plenty. It is the same pure sine wave family as the flagship, rated 1000VA/600W, with the LCD and the USB-HID interface NUT expects, at a noticeably lower price.
 CyberPower CP1000PFCLCD: 600W pure sine, the right size for a single NAS. Image: CyberPower. 
 The trade-off versus the 1500VA unit is runtime headroom. At 600W of real output there is less margin if you later add a second box, so size it for the NAS it protects today and step up if your lab grows.
 Who it’s for: a single NAS plus a switch on a budget, still getting pure sine for the NAS’s PFC power supply. Skip it if: you run a cluster, or you want a long runtime buffer.
 7. CyberPower CP850PFCLCD: best for a low-draw NAS or network shelf
 The smallest pick is for the loads people forget to protect: a two-bay NAS, a mini PC, the router and switch on a networking shelf. The CP850PFCLCD is 850VA/510W, pure sine, with the same LCD and USB monitoring, usually the cheapest unit here.
 CyberPower CP850PFCLCD: 510W pure sine for a small NAS or networking shelf. Image: CyberPower. 
 Keep the load light. At 510W its margin is thin, so this is a single-low-draw-device unit, not something to hang a power-hungry server on. For what it does, it is hard to beat on price while staying pure sine.
 Who it’s for: a mini PC, a two-bay NAS, or networking gear drawing under about 150W. Skip it if: your total load is anywhere near 400W or you want a management card.
 CyberPower CP1500PFCLCD vs APC BR1500MS2
 These two are the most common shortlist for a tower homelab UPS, so here they are side by side from the manufacturers’ spec pages.
 Spec CyberPower CP1500PFCLCD APC BR1500MS2 
 Rating 1500VA / 1000W 1500VA / 900W 
 Waveform on battery Pure sine Pure sine 
 Outlets 12 (6 battery, 6 surge only) 10 (6 battery, 4 surge only) 
 USB charging USB-A + USB-C USB-A + USB-C 
 Network card option Yes (RMCARD205) No 
 NUT driver usbhid-ups usbhid-ups 
 Approx price ~$240 ~$300 
 Specs from CyberPower and Schneider Electric; prices from our October 2026 Amazon check. 
 The CyberPower wins on paper: 100W more real output, two more outlets, a management card slot, and it costs about $60 less. Buy the APC if you already run APC gear elsewhere in the house. Either one does the job with NUT, because both show up as a standard USB HID UPS.
 How to size a UPS for a homelab
 Sizing a homelab UPS takes one measurement and one rule. The measurement is the real wattage of everything you want on battery, taken at the wall rather than guessed from power supply labels, which overstate draw by a wide margin. A plug-in meter like the P3 Kill A Watt EZ (P4460) (about $35) reads watts, amps, and VA for anything up to 15 A, so plug the NAS, the Proxmox node, and the switch in one at a time, or put a power strip behind the meter and read them together under a normal workload.
 The rule: keep that total under about half the UPS’s watt rating, not its VA rating. A “1500VA” label on a unit rated 900W to 1050W is marketing math. Half load leaves headroom for boot surges and a battery that has aged, and it is also the point where manufacturers quote runtime, so you can read the result straight off the spec sheet. A worked example: a four-bay NAS, a mini PC, and a 2.5GbE switch that meter at 180W together sit at 18% of a CP1500PFCLCD’s 1000W. CyberPower quotes 10 minutes at half load (500W), so at 180W you get well over that, and independent tests of this unit have measured more than 25 minutes at around 150W. That covers a clean shutdown several times over.
 One note for readers outside North America: every pick on this page is a 120V model with US outlets. In 230V markets, CyberPower sells the same PFC Sinewave line under E-suffixed model numbers (the CP1350EPFCLCD, for example, is on NUT’s compatibility list), while APC’s 230V ranges differ from the US models, so confirm the on-battery waveform on the local spec page. Match the local model number to the specs above before you buy.
 Set up graceful shutdown with NUT (the part that saves your data)
 Buying the UPS is half the job. The other half is making the server act on it. Network UPS Tools is the standard on Linux, and it has one feature a single-machine tool cannot match: the box with the USB cable can tell every other machine in the lab to shut down too. Here is the setup we ran on Debian 13, which is also what a Proxmox node uses.
 Install the server and client packages. On Debian, Ubuntu, or Proxmox:
 sudo apt update 
sudo apt install -y nut-server nut-client 
 On RHEL, Rocky, AlmaLinux, or Fedora the package is just nut via dnf install -y nut . Next, tell NUT about the UPS. Open the driver config:
 sudo vim /etc/nut/ups.conf 
 Add a section for the UPS. Almost every CyberPower and APC USB unit uses the usbhid-ups driver, and port = auto finds it without you hunting for a device path:
 [ cps ] 
 driver = usbhid-ups
 port = auto
 desc = " Homelab UPS " 
 Run NUT as a network server so other nodes can subscribe to this UPS later. Open the mode file:
 sudo vim /etc/nut/nut.conf 
 Set a single line:
 MODE = netserver 
 Create a monitoring account. Open the users file:
 sudo vim /etc/nut/upsd.users 
 Define a user that upsmon will log in as. Change the password to your own:
 [monuser]
 password = ChangeThisPassword
 upsmon primary 
 Now wire up the monitor itself, which is the piece that decides when to pull the plug gracefully. Open its config:
 sudo vim /etc/nut/upsmon.conf 
 Point it at the UPS and tell it what to run on a forced shutdown. The MONITOR line uses the same user and password you just set:
 MONITOR cps@localhost 1 monuser ChangeThisPassword primary
MINSUPPLIES 1
SHUTDOWNCMD "/sbin/shutdown -h +0"
POLLFREQ 5
POLLFREQALERT 5 
 Start both services and confirm NUT can see the UPS:
 sudo systemctl restart nut-server nut-monitor 
upsc cps 
 You should get the live status back, with the model, battery charge, current load, and a status of OL for online:
 Here is the trick that separates a working setup from one that only looks like it works: test the shutdown logic before a real outage instead of during one. NUT ships a dummy-ups driver that simulates a UPS, so you can flip it to “on battery” and then “low battery” and watch upsmon react, all without touching your real power. In our lab the moment the simulated battery went critical, upsmon logged the on-battery and low-battery events and ran the shutdown command exactly as configured (we pointed it at a log file so the test box stayed up for the screenshot; on a real server it runs your SHUTDOWNCMD , the shutdown -h +0 line above):
 For a cluster, this is where NUT earns its place. The node with the USB cable stays as the primary above. First, on that primary, add a LISTEN 0.0.0.0 3493 line to /etc/nut/upsd.conf and open TCP port 3493, because upsd binds to localhost only by default and the other nodes get a connection refused without it. Every other Proxmox or TrueNAS box then runs only upsmon in secondary mode, pointing its MONITOR line at the primary’s IP instead of localhost . On a low-battery event the secondaries disconnect and shut down first, the primary waits for them, then shuts down last and signals the UPS to cut power. One UPS, one USB cable, the whole lab protected. If you are still planning the storage side of that lab, our guide to the best NAS for home and Plex and the DIY NAS build with TrueNAS or Unraid pair naturally with this.
 UPS shutdown on TrueNAS, Unraid, Synology, and Proxmox
 You only need the manual NUT setup above on a plain Linux box or a Proxmox node, because Proxmox has no UPS settings in its web UI. The NAS platforms have it built in, and each one works a little differently.
 TrueNAS uses NUT under the hood. Enable the UPS service, pick your model’s driver from the list (the CyberPower and APC picks here all use usbhid-ups ), set UPS Mode to Master if the USB cable plugs into the TrueNAS box, and tick Remote Monitor so other machines can subscribe to it as NUT secondaries, the same way the cluster setup above works.
 Unraid ships with apcupsd, not NUT. Its built-in UPS settings work well for an APC unit on USB. apcupsd often works with a CyberPower on USB too, but when it misreads the unit, or when Unraid has to share one UPS with other machines, the usual route is to turn the built-in APC daemon off and install the community NUT plugin, which then behaves like any other NUT primary or secondary.
 Synology DSM has UPS support under Control Panel, Hardware & Power, UPS. Plug the UPS in over USB, tick Enable UPS support, and choose whether the NAS enters Standby Mode at low battery or after a set time. Ticking Enable network UPS server and adding the IPs of your other Synology units lets them shut down off the same UPS. Synology recommends testing it with a real outage simulation first, because the option to power the UPS off after shutdown varies by brand and model.
 Lithium UPS and power stations: are they worth it?
 Every pick above uses sealed lead-acid batteries, which is why you replace them every three to five years. Lithium changes that, but the price gap is still wide. APC’s own lithium Smart-UPS, the SMTL1500RM3UC (a 3U rackmount unit rated 1440VA/1350W), sells for about $1,800 on Amazon, about two and a half times what the lead-acid SMT1500C costs. That only pays off if you really hate battery swaps.
 The cheaper route to lithium, and the most common “homelab UPS alternative” people ask about, is a portable power station with a UPS mode. The one we would pick is the EcoFlow River 3 Plus (about $299). It has a 286Wh LiFePO4 battery, 600W of pure sine output on three UPS-protected AC outlets, a quoted switchover under 10 ms, and a one-hour recharge from the wall. EcoFlow rates the battery for 10 years before it drops to 80% capacity.
 EcoFlow River 3 Plus: 286Wh LiFePO4, 600W pure sine, under 10 ms switchover, USB-B for shutdown signaling. Image: EcoFlow. 
 The catch is shutdown integration. The River 3 Plus has a USB-B port and presents itself as a USB HID UPS, but NUT only added basic support for it (and the Delta 3 Plus) in NUT 2.8.3, and some firmware revisions need a fix that is still in NUT’s development branch. Debian 13 ships NUT 2.8.1, which is what we tested above, so on a stock Debian or Proxmox host you would need a newer NUT build before it can trigger a shutdown. Its switchover is also slower than the 4 ms a line-interactive UPS like the CP1500PFCLCD quotes. ATX power supplies must hold up for at least 12 ms at full load, so a healthy one should ride through a 10 ms gap with little margin to spare. NAS power bricks are not held to that spec, so test it with your own hardware before you trust it with a ZFS pool. For a router and a mini PC it is a great fit; for a storage server, a real UPS is still the safer default.
 What to look for when buying a UPS
 The picks above cover most situations, but if you are comparing other models, these are the axes that decide it.
 Pure sine wave, always, for a server. This is the one to not compromise on. Avoid the units sold as “simulated”, “stepped”, or “approximated” sine wave for anything with an Active PFC power supply, which is every modern server and NAS. The popular APC Back-UPS BX1500M and the CyberPower CP1500AVRLCD3 are both simulated-sine units per their own spec pages, and the Eaton 5S1500LCD is widely reported as one too (Eaton does not publish its waveform, so confirm it before buying). They are fine for a lamp or a basic desktop, but a PFC supply can shut down the instant they switch to battery. Every pick on this page is pure sine for exactly this reason.
 Size by watts, not VA. A “1500VA” unit usually delivers only 900W to 1050W of real power because of its power factor. Measure your real draw and keep it under about half the watt rating, as covered in the sizing section above.
 Runtime is a calculator, not a spec. The “10 minutes” on the box is at half load. Use the manufacturer’s runtime calculator with your actual watt draw. You do not need an hour; you need enough to trigger and complete a clean shutdown, which is usually two to five minutes. Long runtime only matters if you want the lab to ride through short outages without shutting down at all.
 Confirm NUT support. Every pick here uses the usbhid-ups driver, which is the most widely supported path and what TrueNAS and Proxmox expect. Before buying anything off this list, check the model against the official NUT hardware compatibility list . For APC units specifically, use NUT rather than the older apcupsd; NUT is actively maintained and lets multiple machines monitor one UPS, and you should never run both daemons on the same box.
 Batteries are consumable. Every UPS battery degrades and needs replacing every three to five years. Tower units like the CyberPowers use sealed packs you swap yourself after powering down; the Smart-UPS and both rack CyberPowers use hot-swappable cartridges you can replace without dropping the load. Factor a replacement into the long-term cost, and test your runtime once a year so you are not surprised by a battery that has quietly died.
 Pairs with Best NAS Case (2026): Mini-ITX to 12-Bay TrueNAS Chassis 
 Best Synology Alternatives: UGREEN vs QNAP vs UniFi UNAS vs DIY 
 ZimaCube 2 NAS Guide: Drives, RAID, Review Data 
 Which one to pick
 For most homelabs, the CyberPower CP1500PFCLCD is the answer: pure sine, 1000W, the cleanest NUT integration, and the price is right. Drop to the CP1000PFCLCD if you are protecting a single NAS and want to spend less, or the CP850PFCLCD for a low-draw shelf. Put it in a rack and the CP1500PFCRM2U is the same idea in 2U for about $360; step up to the OR1500PFCRT2U only if you want the lab to keep running through a longer outage. Spend up to the APC Smart-UPS SMT1500C only when long runtime, a hot-swap battery, and a network management card genuinely matter, such as a cluster you cannot afford to lose. Whichever you buy, spend the twenty minutes to wire up NUT and run the dummy-ups test, because the UPS that does not shut your server down cleanly is just an expensive surge strip. Once the power side is sorted, the right NAS drives and a tuned ZFS pool layout are what your clean shutdown is protecting.

Best UPS for NAS 2026: Which One Do You Actually Need? 
 Skip to content 
 Best UPS for NAS 2026: What You Actually Need
 Updated: 2026-07-02 · Last verified July 2026 
 TL;DR A 4-bay home NAS is happy on an 800-1000 VA line-interactive UPS with pure sine wave output and a USB data link. The picks below cover a small 2-bay setup, a Ugreen NASync DC-UPS, and a 1500 VA unit for 4-8 bay builds, all listed on Synology's compatibility page or supported by NUT for TrueNAS, Unraid and OpenMediaVault.
 A UPS isn't a nice-to-have on a NAS, it's the difference between a graceful shutdown and a filesystem that boots into a degraded pool. If you're shopping for your first NAS or picking one up in the same order, the smart move is to plan the UPS at the same time so the VA rating actually matches what your box will draw. This guide walks through the sizing math, explains why pure sine wave keeps showing up in the requirements, and lists the four units worth buying in 2026.
 Sizing your NAS first? Plan disks + RAID, the calculator shows power draw estimate per pool. 
 Open calculator → 
 Why a UPS is mandatory for a NAS
 A NAS isn't a PC. When the power drops mid-write, the drives don't just lose the current file: the RAID layer may have already committed the data block but not the parity update, which leaves the array in an inconsistent state that only a full controlled shutdown avoids. On ZFS you'll usually recover thanks to the transactional design, but on hardware RAID or old ext4-on-mdadm you can end up rebuilding the whole pool, and Btrfs' RAID 5/6 layer still has known write-hole edge cases that a clean shutdown sidesteps.
 The second reason is what utility engineers politely call "dirty power". Brownouts, voltage sags and the short spikes that follow a lightning strike a few streets over don't kill the drive today; they age the electronics faster and cause the SATA controller to log recoverable read errors that would never appear on a clean line. A line-interactive UPS clamps that noise before it reaches the PSU, so the same drives simply last longer.
 The third reason is the one nobody plans for: brownout loops. When the grid dips just below the PSU's cut-off threshold every few seconds during a bad storm, the NAS reboots on a loop, and every reboot spins the drives back up from parked heads. One thunderstorm night on a raw wall socket can eat months of expected drive life, whereas a UPS just rides it out on battery. That alone is why every NAS vendor recommends one.
 How to size the VA rating
 The sizing math is simpler than the datasheets make it look. Take the wall-plug draw of your NAS in watts, multiply by 1.6 to convert to volt-amps at a typical power factor of around 0.62, then multiply by 1.3 as a safety margin so the UPS isn't running at its rated limit. That gives you the minimum VA you should shop for; from there you buy up one size for headroom and runtime, because runtime falls off a cliff as you approach the rated capacity.
 Some worked examples that map to the NAS most people actually own:
 2-bay Synology DS224+ plus a small switch, roughly 30 W total: 30 × 1.6 × 1.3 ≈ 62 VA, so a 350-600 VA unit is plenty.
 4-bay DS923+ with four 16 TB drives, roughly 50 W: 50 × 1.6 × 1.3 ≈ 104 VA, so a 600-1000 VA unit gives you real runtime instead of just headroom.
 8-bay DIY build with a Ryzen 5 and eight 18 TB drives, roughly 110 W: 110 × 1.6 × 1.3 ≈ 230 VA, so a 1000-1500 VA unit is the sensible floor.
 The reason to buy more VA than you strictly need is runtime. Five to ten minutes on battery covers a normal DSM or TrueNAS shutdown with time to spare; twenty to thirty minutes lets you ride through most short outages without shutting down at all, which is nice-to-have but not required.
 Want this worked out for your gear? Add every device you plan to protect and see the VA rating plus realistic runtime. 
 Open UPS calculator → 
 UPS topologies that actually matter
 UPS marketing loves to invent topology names, but for a home NAS the choice really is just three. The cheapest is offline (standby), where the battery only kicks in once the wall power fails; the switch-over gap is around 10 ms, which is fine for a desktop PC but marginal for a NAS with an Active PFC power supply that can hiccup on that gap.
 Line-interactive is the sweet spot for home storage. It adds automatic voltage regulation (AVR) that trims brownouts and swells without going to battery at all, and the switch-over when it does dip is closer to 3-5 ms, well inside what a modern NAS PSU rides through. Every unit recommended below is line-interactive for exactly this reason.
 Online (double-conversion) UPSes rectify the wall power to DC and re-invert it continuously, so the load never sees a transition: the switch time is effectively zero. They're excellent, they're also loud, expensive and overkill for a home NAS. Save them for a small server rack or a lab where a hiccup mid-workload is genuinely unacceptable.
 Pure sine wave versus modified sine wave
 Cheap UPSes save cost by approximating the AC waveform with a stepped square wave, marketed as "modified sine wave". That works fine for resistive loads and older PSUs, but modern NAS power supplies use Active Power Factor Correction, and Active PFC circuits can misread the stepped waveform as a fault and either shut down or draw huge inrush currents that trip the UPS. Synology's own UPS support article and the compatibility list both flag pure sine wave as the safe default. The premium over a modified-sine equivalent is small enough that there's no reason to gamble.
 Synology and NUT compatibility
 For the NAS to actually shut down cleanly when the battery runs low, it needs to talk to the UPS over USB. Synology maintains an official UPS compatibility list which is the shortest path if you're on DSM: pick a model that's on it and the driver is baked in. TrueNAS, Unraid and OpenMediaVault use Network UPS Tools (NUT) instead, and the stable HCL lists every driver-model combination that's known to work. Check whichever list applies to your OS before you click buy; it's a two-minute step that saves the "why won't my NAS see the UPS" evening.
 For the more technical crowd: NUT drivers matter more than you'd think. The generic usbhid-ups driver handles most modern APC and Eaton units, but CyberPower's older CP-series need the cyberpower or blazer_usb driver, and Ugreen's US3000 speaks a Megatec-style protocol that NUT talks to via blazer_usb . If a model works on DSM but not on TrueNAS, that mismatch is almost always the reason.
 Ubiquiti's UNAS units are the exception to most of the advice above. Graceful shutdown on a UniFi UNAS is built around Ubiquiti's own rackmount UniFi UPS, which signals UNAS and UNVR devices directly, rather than around the USB cable and NUT arrangement the rest of this article assumes, and third-party USB support has been a standing community request rather than a shipped feature. There is one tidy consequence for the small models: the UNAS 2 and UNAS 4 take their power over Ethernet, so protecting them is really a matter of putting the switch behind a UPS, which you should be doing regardless.
 Direct-buy: our 2026 UPS picks
 Amazon affiliate links. As Amazon Associates we earn from qualifying purchases, at no extra cost to you.
 Small NAS · 600 VA APC Back-UPS BE600M1 600 VA / 330 W, USB monitoring; covers a 2-bay NAS plus switch. Check price → 
 Ugreen NASync · DC UPS Ugreen US3000 UPS DC UPS designed for Ugreen NASync DXP/DH models, vendor-rated at 120 W. Check price → 
 4-8 bay · 1500 VA CyberPower CP1500EPFCLCD 1500 VA / 900 W pure sine, AVR, USB, user-replaceable battery. Check price → 
 Homelab · 1500 VA Eaton 5E 1500 Line-interactive 1500 VA, USB, works with NUT and DSM. Check price → 
 What to avoid
 The trap on the shelf is any generic offline UPS priced under €70 or so: those almost always ship with modified sine wave output, no USB signalling and a soldered-in battery that's toast in one or two years. You save fifty euros up front and buy a new unit twice as often, which is bad value even before the risk to the NAS. Anything without a user-replaceable battery is a similar false economy, because the battery is the one component guaranteed to fail on a fixed schedule.
 The other thing to skip is any pitch that sells a modified-sine UPS as "compatible with Synology" without appearing on Synology's own list. Vendors are explicit in their support docs that Active PFC power supplies expect pure sine wave, and running them off a stepped waveform is grounds for the warranty conversation you don't want to have.
 Setup checklist
 Once the box arrives, the sequence that keeps everyone out of trouble is straightforward:
 Plug the UPS into a wall socket and let it charge for at least eight hours before loading it.
 Connect the USB data cable from the UPS to a free port on the NAS.
 In DSM, open Control Panel → Hardware & Power → UPS and enable UPS support; on Unraid, enable UPS support under Settings → UPS Settings; on TrueNAS, enable the NUT service, and in both cases confirm it detects the model.
 Set the shutdown trigger to either "30 seconds before battery empty" or "5 minutes on battery", whichever your outage profile fits better.
 Test it: with the NAS running, pull the UPS plug from the wall and confirm the NAS reaches a clean shutdown before the battery gives out.
 Recommendation
 For most home NAS setups the sensible default is the CyberPower CP1500EPFCLCD paired with a 4-bay box, because 1500 VA of pure sine gives you real runtime margin and the user-replaceable battery keeps the same chassis alive for five-plus years. If you're on a 2-bay DS224+ or similar and the budget is tight, the APC BE600M1 covers the shutdown case cleanly; if you're on the Ugreen NASync line, the US3000 DC-UPS is the model that actually integrates with the box. Homelab racks and anyone running TrueNAS with NUT will be happier with the Eaton 5E 1500, which is a plain, quiet, long-lived unit that just works.
 Frequently asked questions
 What size UPS do I need for my NAS? Rule of thumb: NAS watts × 1.6 × 1.3 = required VA. A 4-bay NAS at 50 W needs around 600-800 VA for 5-10 minutes of runtime. An 8-bay DIY at 110 W needs 1000-1500 VA.
 Do I need pure sine wave for my NAS? Synology explicitly recommends it. Modern NAS power supplies use Active PFC which can struggle with modified sine wave. When in doubt: buy pure sine wave.
 Which UPS is Synology compatible? Synology maintains an official compatibility list. APC Back-UPS, CyberPower and Eaton models are all on it. Verify your exact model before buying.
 How long does a UPS battery last? Typically 3-5 years. After that the capacity drops. Models with user-replaceable batteries save money long-term because you swap the battery instead of tossing the whole unit.
 Is a cheap offline UPS enough? Fine for a PC, marginal for NAS. The 8-12 ms switch may work, but modified sine wave and no USB signalling make a clean shutdown impossible.

 Specifications and transfer times below come from the makers and NUT project; runtime examples are calculated assumptions.
 Quick picks: which battery fits your job?
 Best UPS-mode power station: EcoFlow RIVER 3 Max. Its RIVER 3 Plus base has a maker-rated under-10 ms transfer and a USB-B communication port. The 572 Wh package adds an EB300 battery. It is the strongest fit here for networking plus a computer or NAS, with a shutdown test as part of setup.
 Best for a router only: EcoFlow RIVER 3 230Wh. You get ordinary AC output in a smaller battery package. EcoFlow explicitly excludes NAS and other uninterrupted computer loads from this version’s intended use.
 Best capacity: BLUETTI AC180. Its 1,152 Wh battery is the largest here. Choose it when longer runtime matters and your equipment tolerates its 20 ms transfer with Grid Enhancement off ; its AC inverter’s own consumption matters at router-sized loads.
 For portable DC devices: Anker SOLIX C300 DC. This is a 288 Wh DC-only battery, with no AC outlets and no published UPS transfer figure in the maker guide we checked. Buy it for compatible USB/DC devices, not as a drop-in NAS UPS.

 Use continuous output ratings for electronics. EcoFlow’s X-Boost heating-appliance claims and BLUETTI’s lifting-mode headline are not extra normal AC capacity for your NAS.
 Will UPS mode switch fast enough?
 Pass-through means the station can supply a load while connected to input power. Transfer time tells you how long the interruption is when that input disappears. Those are different buying questions.
 The RIVER 3 Max has the best published transfer figure among these AC candidates. EcoFlow’s Plus manual describes the base unit as a standby UPS with transfer within 10 ms; its US page advertises under 10 ms. Choose it first for the UPS-mode job, then test the actual equipment.
 For comparison, the line-interactive CyberPower CP1500PFCLCDa has a maker-listed typical 4 ms transfer, automatic voltage regulation and USB management. “Typical” and a maximum-style claim are different specifications, so don’t turn those numbers into an exact speed ratio. Our NAS UPS buying guide covers pure versus stepped sine, USB/NUT evidence and setup for TrueNAS, Unraid and Synology; the CyberPower specifications explain the conventional UPS option.
 A router’s power brick may ride through a short gap, but the way to find out is a controlled transfer test. A NAS also needs time to stop writes and shut down. That makes communication just as important as fast switching.
 Skip RIVER 3 230 for a NAS. Its manual specifically tells you not to connect NAS servers, desktops and similar devices requiring uninterrupted supply. Its 20 ms EPS feature is useful for suitable loads; it does not make it the same product as the Plus/Max.
 How long will your router, ONT and NAS run?
 Start with a plug-in power meter , not the power brick’s maximum label. Measure the equipment together, including any switch needed to keep it useful. For a NAS, include a busy period and drive startup in your output-capacity check.
 Here is a planning worksheet with deliberately stated inputs:
 Router plus modem: 20 W combined .
 Add an optical network terminal, or ONT: 10 W , taking the total to 30 W . Include this only if your connection actually uses one alongside those devices.
 Add a mini PC: 20 W , taking the total to 50 W .
 Add a two-bay NAS: 30 W , taking the total to 80 W .
 These are assumed loads, not typical-use measurements. For every AC example, assume 90% usable battery, 85% inverter efficiency and 15 W fixed station overhead . The AC180 manual uses this calculation structure, quotes about 15 W self-consumption and gives 90% depth of discharge with inverter efficiency above 85%. Applying those same values to EcoFlow is a comparison assumption, not an EcoFlow efficiency specification.

 RIVER 3 Max is the exception worth knowing about. Its Plus base has a USB-B data port, and EcoFlow documents Power Manager software for PC/NAS monitoring and automatic shutdown. Separately, NUT’s hardware compatibility list lists RIVER 3 Plus over USB with usbhid-ups .

Use a NUT package that includes the model’s support, connect the data cable and verify that the host sees mains loss, battery state and the shutdown event. A NAS appliance’s bundled NUT version and device list can differ from the current project list.
 The AC180, RIVER 3 230 and C300 DC manuals checked here do not document a USB UPS management interface. Their USB charging sockets cannot supply a battery-status signal simply because a cable fits. If automatic NAS shutdown is your priority, choose the Max’s supported communication route or a conventional managed UPS.
 Our UPS sizing and graceful-shutdown guide walks through the complete dependency chain: the protected host, the controller and any networking needed to deliver the shutdown command. A battery can keep supplying power long after a host has lost the network path it needs.
 Where the C300 DC makes sense
 The Anker A1726 guide lists USB-C outputs and a 12 V, 10 A car socket. It suits compatible portable devices, including USB-C equipment that accepts the offered power profile. It does not accept a router’s AC power brick.
 For a barrel-powered router, voltage, connector, polarity and current all have to match through a suitable regulated power arrangement. Don’t turn this purchase into an improvised cable project. An AC-output station lets you retain the equipment’s original power adapters instead.
 The maker guide publishes no UPS switchover figure or seamless pass-through commitment for this DC model. It also documents low-current USB auto-off behavior after two hours. Choose it as portable backup, and choose one of the AC UPS-mode options when automatic changeover is the job.
 Set it up before the first storm
 For off-grid texts, choose a battery-powered Meshtastic starter node and test messages with a second node before the next outage.
 Choose the protected load. Keep the list short: internet equipment first, then a host or NAS with a clear shutdown job. Measure watts and use the sizing guide for W/VA headroom.
 Give the station ventilation. Follow its manual’s placement and charging instructions; keep intake and exhaust clear.
 Set UPS and low-load options. On AC180, turn Grid Enhancement off in the BLUETTI app: the manual’s page 13 says it lengthens switchover when enabled. Disable AC ECO auto-off for an always-on small load too. On EcoFlow RIVER 3 230 and the Plus base in Max, set AC timeout to Never in the EcoFlow app so an idle outlet stays on.
 Connect shutdown data where supported. On Max, use the Plus base’s USB-B communication port, then configure and verify the software on the actual protected host.
 Test a mains failure. Follow the maker’s outage-test procedure with nonessential workloads first. Watch whether the router reboots, the host reports battery operation and the NAS completes an orderly shutdown with charge remaining.
 Test recovery too. Restore input power and observe charging, outlet state and host restart behavior. Write down what needs a button press so the next outage has fewer surprises.
 Buy RIVER 3 Max for the most complete UPS-mode package here, RIVER 3 230 for suitable router-only duty, or AC180 for the larger energy reserve. Keep C300 DC on the portable-DC shortlist.
