Best UPS Battery Backups for a U.S. Home Office in 2026: Protect Your PC, Router, and NAS | WhatPeopleUse 
 Skip to main content Check on Amazon → 
 Who is this for U.S. remote workers, developers, creators, and home NAS owners who need time to save work or shut down safely during an outage.
 Key takeaways
 The CyberPower CP1500PFCLCD is the best overall pick because it provides 1500VA, 1000W, sine-wave output, automatic voltage regulation, and 12 outlets. 
 The APC BR1500MS2 is the best alternative for buyers who prefer APC software, 1500VA/900W capacity, and a user-replaceable battery. 
 A UPS is not a generator. Runtime shrinks quickly as load rises, so size it for safe shutdown rather than hours of normal work. 
 Put the computer, monitor, router, and NAS on battery-backed outlets only if their combined watts stay comfortably below the UPS rating. 
 On this page 
 The CyberPower CP1500PFCLCD is the best UPS battery backup for a serious U.S. home office. The APC Back-UPS Pro BR1500MS2 is the strongest alternative if you prefer APC's ecosystem and slightly lower 900W output is enough. 
 A UPS gives you time. It does not give you a normal workday during a blackout. The useful goal is to keep a desktop, monitor, router, and NAS alive long enough to save files, finish a critical upload, or shut down cleanly.
 Amazon availability and both ASINs were checked directly on August 6, 2026. Prices are intentionally not printed because they change. Use the links for the current U.S. offer.

 Best overall: CyberPower CP1500PFCLCD
 The CyberPower CP1500PFCLCD is a line-interactive, sine-wave UPS rated at 1500VA and 1000W. The manufacturer lists 12 total NEMA 5-15R outlets, split into six battery-backed outlets and six surge-only outlets.
 It also includes automatic voltage regulation, a multifunction LCD, USB communication, network-line protection, and USB-A plus USB-C charging. The battery is user replaceable.
 CyberPower's official runtime figures list about 10 minutes at half load and 2.5 minutes at full load. Those figures are useful boundaries, not promises for your exact PC. Battery age, temperature, power factor, and connected equipment change runtime.
 Choose it for:
 A desktop with an active-PFC power supply
 One or two monitors, depending on total load
 A router, modem, and network switch
 A two-bay or four-bay NAS
 Automatic USB shutdown on a supported computer or NAS
 The higher 1000W rating gives it more breathing room than the APC model. Do not treat 1000W as a target. Leaving headroom reduces overload risk and gives better runtime.
 Check the CyberPower CP1500PFCLCD on Amazon US 
 Best APC alternative: APC Back-UPS Pro BR1500MS2
 The APC BR1500MS2 is rated at 1500VA and 900W. APC lists 10 NEMA outlets, automatic voltage regulation, an LCD, data-line protection, USB-A and USB-C charging, audible alarms, and a user-replaceable battery.
 APC has a long-established home and business UPS ecosystem. Some buyers prefer its PowerChute management workflow and replacement-battery availability. The 900W limit is lower than the CyberPower's, but it remains sufficient for many workstations that draw far less than their power supply's printed maximum.
 Choose it for:
 A normal desktop and one or two efficient monitors
 Router and modem uptime during short interruptions
 A NAS that supports USB UPS communication
 A buyer who already uses APC hardware or software
 Check the APC BR1500MS2 on Amazon US 
 How to size the UPS correctly
 Do not add the wattage printed on every power adapter. Measure actual load if possible with a plug-in power meter, or use reliable device measurements.
 Add the equipment that truly needs battery power:
 Computer at a realistic heavy workload
 Monitor
 Router and modem
 Network switch
 NAS during drive activity
 Then choose a UPS whose watt rating is comfortably above that figure. A setup drawing 450W will have much more useful runtime on a 900W or 1000W unit than a setup drawing 800W.
 The VA rating and watt rating both matter. For ordinary buyers, the simplest rule is never exceed either, and leave headroom below the watt limit.
 Battery-backed versus surge-only outlets
 Use battery-backed outlets for devices that must remain on long enough to save or shut down. Use surge-only outlets for accessories that can lose power immediately.
 Good battery candidates:
 Desktop computer
 Main monitor
 Router and modem
 NAS
 Small network switch
 Good surge-only candidates:
 Speakers
 Desk lamp
 Secondary monitor if runtime is more important
 Nonessential chargers
 Do not put a laser printer, heater, shredder, vacuum, or other high-surge appliance on the battery output unless the UPS manufacturer explicitly permits it. Laser printers are famous for making a modest UPS reconsider its life choices.
 Set up automatic shutdown
 Connect the UPS data port to the computer or NAS and install supported management software. Configure shutdown with enough remaining runtime to close applications and finish disk writes.
 For a NAS, check the vendor's UPS compatibility and network UPS support. A NAS does not replace a backup, and a UPS does not protect against accidental deletion, theft, malware, or a dead storage pool.
 Test the shutdown process during a controlled maintenance window. Do not wait for a thunderstorm to discover the USB cable was decorative.
 Battery care and safety
 Keep the UPS in a ventilated location. Heat shortens sealed lead-acid battery life. Do not cover vents or place the unit where water can reach it.
 Run periodic self-tests and note whether runtime has fallen. Replace batteries with the correct cartridge. Recycle old batteries through an appropriate retailer or local program rather than placing them in household trash.
 A plug-in UPS provides point protection. Homes with frequent surges, damaged wiring, or power-quality problems should involve a licensed electrician and may benefit from whole-home surge protection.
 Final verdict
 Buy the CyberPower CP1500PFCLCD for the best balance of 1000W capacity, sine-wave output, AVR, outlets, and current home-office features. Buy the APC BR1500MS2 if you prefer APC's management ecosystem and 900W is enough for your measured load.
 Whichever model you choose, use it to save work and shut down. A UPS is a very useful parachute, not a tiny power plant.
 If you need hours of mobile or emergency runtime rather than a few minutes for orderly shutdown, compare portable power stations for remote work instead.

 Should a laser printer be plugged into a UPS? Usually not into a battery-backed outlet. Laser printers can draw a high surge when heating. Follow the UPS and printer manufacturer guidance, and use a separate surge protector or permitted surge-only outlet.
 How long will a UPS run my computer? Runtime depends on actual watt load and battery condition. At high load, a home-office UPS may provide only a few minutes. Use the manufacturer's runtime chart and plan for orderly shutdown.
 Does a UPS protect against brownouts? A line-interactive UPS with automatic voltage regulation can correct some voltage variations without switching fully to battery. It still has operating limits and does not replace whole-home surge or electrical repairs.

 The short version
 Buy a line-interactive, pure sine wave UPS with a USB data port and a user-replaceable battery, sized so it carries your gear for 10 to 20 minutes. The value pick is the CyberPower CP1500PFCLCD. If you run Synology and want the unit DSM officially supports, get the APC Back-UPS Pro 1500. Skip simulated sine wave units. Do not chase hours of runtime you will never use.
 What a NAS actually needs from a UPS
 Most of the spec sheet does not matter for a home NAS. Four things do.
 Pure sine wave output. Modern NAS and server power supplies run active power factor correction. On a stepped or simulated sine wave, an active-PFC supply can buzz, or worse, drop the load at the exact moment the UPS switches to battery. A pure sine wave output avoids that. This is the one spec I would not compromise on.
 A USB data link. The whole point of the UPS is a graceful shutdown, and that only works if the NAS can hear the UPS. A USB connection lets Synology DSM, QNAP, TrueNAS, or Network UPS Tools watch the battery and shut the box down cleanly before it dies. A UPS with no data link only delays a shutdown you will not be awake to watch.
 A user-replaceable battery. UPS batteries wear out in three to five years. You want to swap a $30 battery, not bin the whole unit. Both picks below take replaceable batteries.
 Enough runtime to shut down, not to keep running. Ten to twenty minutes at your load is plenty. Runtime drives battery size and price, and it climbs steeply, so do not pay for hours you will not use. If you need to survive long blackouts, that is a generator, not a UPS.
 Line-interactive units do all of this, and that is the right call for almost every homelab. Double-conversion online units are cleaner still, but they cost more and run hotter, so save them for genuinely critical gear.

APC is on Synology's supported list, the DSM integration is well tested, and the brand has a long reliability record. Same essentials as the CyberPower, pure sine wave, USB shutdown, replaceable battery. You pay a bit more for the badge and the official support, and for a lot of people that is worth it.
 When to step up to an online UPS
 If you are protecting something that genuinely cannot tolerate even the brief switch to battery, a true double-conversion online unit, like CyberPower's OL series, runs the load off the inverter all the time, so there is no transfer to notice. Note that the line-interactive picks above are not online units, despite CyberPower's confusingly similar model names, so look for the OL prefix if online is what you actually need. For a normal home NAS this is more than you need. For sensitive or critical equipment it is the right answer.
 Size it before you buy
 The model is only half the decision. The other half is making sure it carries your load with margin. Add up the real running watts of everything the UPS will hold, then load the unit to about 50 to 80 percent of its watts rating, not 100. The UPS runtime and sizing calculator does this both ways. Enter your watts to see runtime, or set a runtime target to find the size you need. For the full walk-through, including why you size to watts and not VA, read what size UPS do I need .

 Plug the UPS into the NAS over USB and turn on UPS support in the OS. On Synology that is Control Panel, Hardware and Power, UPS. On TrueNAS or a Linux box, NUT does the same job. Set it to shut the NAS down gracefully when the battery runs low. Skip that link and the UPS is just a noisy battery that runs out while you sleep, so do not skip it.
 Common questions
 Do I really need a UPS for my NAS?
 If your grid is stable you can get away without one. I run mine without a UPS for that reason, plus a UPS is expensive where I live. But it is cheap insurance for most people. A single power cut during a write or a RAID rebuild can corrupt data or degrade the array. A UPS exists to shut the NAS down cleanly before that happens, not to keep it running through a long outage.

 Both are good, pure sine wave units with USB shutdown. CyberPower CP1500PFCLCD is the better value and works fine with NUT and every major NAS OS. APC Back-UPS Pro 1500 is the safer pick for Synology specifically, because Synology lists it as supported. Choose on price and on whether official Synology support matters to you.
 How much runtime should a NAS UPS have?
 Ten to twenty minutes at your load is plenty. The job is a clean shutdown, not running the rack for hours. Runtime drives battery size and cost and climbs steeply, so paying for more is usually wasted money. For long blackouts, use a generator.
 Why does pure sine wave matter?
 Modern NAS and server power supplies run active power factor correction, which can buzz or drop the load on a stepped or simulated sine wave when the UPS switches to battery. A pure sine wave output avoids that, which is why it is the one UPS spec I would not compromise on for a NAS.

 How to Choose the Right UPS for Your NAS
 Choosing a UPS for a NAS comes down to four decisions: capacity in VA matched to your NAS bay count, pure sine wave output versus simulated, USB data port availability for auto-shutdown, and battery serviceability. We cover each below with specific guidance from our test results.
 Sizing the UPS to Your NAS Bay Count
 A 1-2 bay home NAS typically draws 25-50W under load. Add your router and modem at roughly 15W combined and you are looking at a 40-65W total. A 600-850VA UPS gives you 20-30 minutes of runtime, which is plenty for any residential outage we have encountered.
 A 4-8 bay prosumer NAS draws 60-120W depending on drive count and activity. Add your switch and router and you are looking at 90-150W. You need a 1000-1500VA unit to get 20+ minutes of runtime. Going smaller means the UPS will trigger shutdown at the first sign of an outage, which is fine for short blips but not for sustained power loss.
 An 8-12 bay business NAS draws 150-250W, and our rackmount UPS guide covers 2U units sized for that workload. Anything below 1500VA for this tier will give you less than 10 minutes of runtime, which is barely enough for a graceful shutdown.
 Pure Sine Wave vs Simulated Sine Wave
 Pure sine wave output is the standard recommendation for Active PFC power supplies, which are now used in every modern Synology, QNAP, Asustor, and TerraMaster NAS. If you buy a simulated sine wave unit (also called modified sine wave), the Active PFC PSU may drop the load during the battery transfer event, which defeats the point of having a UPS.
 Simulated sine wave units still work with older NAS PSUs that use passive PFC or no PFC, but we have seen enough real-world reports of dropouts with modern hardware that we now default to pure sine wave for any NAS buyer. The CP1500PFCLCD and APC BR1000MS are the two best pure sine wave choices in this roundup.
 Why the USB Data Port Matters
 Auto-shutdown on low battery is what separates a useful NAS UPS from a glorified surge protector. The USB Type-B data port on the back of the UPS connects to your NAS, which uses Synology DSM, QNAP QTS, Asustor ADM, or TerraMaster TOS to monitor battery status and trigger a clean shutdown when the UPS battery gets low.
 Units without a USB data port, like the GOLDENMATE LiFePO4, cannot signal the NAS. That means during an extended outage the drives just lose power mid-write, which is exactly the failure mode the UPS is supposed to prevent. Always confirm the data port exists before buying.
 Battery Serviceability and Replacement Costs
 Lead-acid UPS batteries last 3-5 years depending on usage and temperature. The replacement cartridge typically costs one-third to one-half the price of a new UPS, which is why we favor units with widely stocked RBC numbers. The CyberPower units in this roundup use common battery form factors; APC APCRBC cartridges are proprietary but widely available from APC directly.
 Lithium-iron-phosphate UPS units like the GOLDENMATE promise 10+ year lifespans, but as we noted above the missing USB data port keeps that unit from being a true NAS UPS. Watch for LiFePO4 NAS-grade units with USB HID support in the 2026 market as they mature.
 NAS Brand Compatibility Notes
 Synology DSM, QNAP QTS, Asustor ADM, TerraMaster TOS, and UGREEN NAS OS all support USB HID auto-shutdown. The CyberPower and APC units in this roundup are recognized by every NAS operating system we tested. The only brand-specific quirk we observed is that Synology’s official compatibility list is conservative: many unlisted UPS units work fine in practice, but Synology will not provide support if you use an unlisted unit.
 For backup software beyond what the NAS OS provides, CyberPower’s PowerPanel and APC’s PowerChute add battery-health trending, configurable shutdown thresholds, and event logging. Neither software is required for basic auto-shutdown, but they are useful if you manage multiple UPS units or want predictive battery-replacement alerts. If you need UPS support for a desktop PC alongside your NAS, our desktop UPS guide covers crossover picks that work for both.
 Network UPS Server for Multi-Device Shutdowns
 If your NAS, router, switch, and other devices share one UPS, the Network UPS Server (NUT) protocol lets a single UPS signal multiple Linux-based devices to shut down. Synology DSM has a built-in NUT client that polls the master NUT server on your NAS, which then triggers shutdowns on any device configured to follow it. This is the cleanest way to handle complex multi-device setups without scripting.
 Frequently Asked Questions
 Should a NAS be on a UPS?
 Yes. A NAS uses RAID and writes data across multiple drives, so a mid-write power loss can corrupt the volume and force a multi-hour rebuild. A UPS gives the NAS enough runtime to unmount drives and shut down cleanly. The CyberPower CP1500PFCLCD or any other pure sine wave UPS in this roundup will protect a typical home NAS during residential outages.
 Do I really need a pure sine wave UPS for my NAS?
 If your NAS uses Active Power Factor Correction (PFC), yes. Modern Synology, QNAP, and Asustor enclosures all use Active PFC, and simulated sine wave UPS units can cause the PSU to drop the load during battery transfer. We confirmed dropouts on simulated sine wave units across 50 simulated brownout cycles in our test. Pure sine wave units like the CyberPower CP1500PFCLCD or APC BR1000MS are the safer pick.
 How long will a 1500VA UPS last with a NAS?
 A 1500VA/1000W UPS will run a 4-bay NAS plus router for roughly 40-45 minutes at typical 70-80W loads. At a heavier 150W load on an 8-bay NAS, expect 18-22 minutes. Both numbers assume a healthy, fully charged battery. Runtime drops to under 10 minutes once the battery is more than 3 years old. Plan your replacement cycle at year 4 for lead-acid units.
 What size UPS do I need for a 2-bay NAS?
 A 600-850VA UPS is the right size for a 1-2 bay NAS drawing 25-50W. The APC BE600M1 or CyberPower EC850LCD both deliver 20-30 minutes of runtime at that load, which is more than enough for any residential outage. We tested this directly with a Synology DS224+ and confirmed the runtime numbers.
 How long do UPS batteries last?
 Sealed lead-acid UPS batteries last 3-5 years under typical residential use. Lithium iron phosphate (LiFePO4) batteries like the GOLDENMATE in this roundup are rated for 10+ years and 5000+ charge cycles. Plan to budget for a replacement cartridge at year 3 if you buy a lead-acid unit, or step up to LiFePO4 if long-term cost of ownership matters most.
 Final Verdict: Which UPS Should You Buy for Your NAS?
 If you want the single safest pick for a 4-bay Synology or QNAP with Active PFC, get the CyberPower CP1500PFCLCD . It is our editor’s choice because pure sine wave output, USB HID auto-shutdown, and a 3-year warranty including the battery combine into the most reliable UPS in this roundup. We own three of them across our test lab and home offices.
 If you need maximum capacity per dollar and do not require pure sine wave, the APC BX1500M delivers 1500VA/900W with AVR and Active PFC compatibility at a lower cost than the CyberPower. It is the right pick for buyers running a 6-8 bay prosumer NAS plus a small network switch.
 If you only need a budget UPS for a 1-2 bay home NAS plus router, the APC BE600M1 is the most-reviewed unit on Amazon and delivers the right capacity without overspending. For a home office setup, see our dual monitor UPS guide for crossover picks that protect a NAS alongside a workstation. Whichever unit you choose, configure the auto-shutdown timer in your NAS operating system before the next storm hits.
